The Violet-chested hummingbird (Sternoclyta cyanopectus) is a relatively large and poorly known trochilid endemic to the Coastal Cordillera and adjacent Andean slopes of northern Venezuela. Hatchlings emerge from eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], with the incubation period culminating in an age at birth of 20.4 days [ab = 20.4 days]. This comparatively protracted embryonic development aligns with the species' montane habitat, where cooler nocturnal temperatures may slow metabolic processes within the egg. A comprehensive captive-rearing study reported that freshly hatched nestlings weighed a mere 0.33 grams [Wwb = 0.33 grams], reflecting the extreme altricial condition typical of hummingbirds. The limited yolk reserves of the newly hatched chick are supplemented almost immediately by intensive parental provisioning, allowing for a rapid phase of mass gain. The adult body mass for this species, representing the ultimate wet weight, has been recorded at 7.5 grams [Wwi = 7.5 grams], a figure consistent with several other medium-sized cloud-forest hummingbirds and indicative of the energetic demands of hovering flight in dense vegetation.

Under the elevated body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] that characterizes the active, homeothermic phase of adult hummingbirds, several critical life-history transitions have been documented. The time since birth at fledging, marking the successful achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest, is estimated at 26 days [tx = 26 days] at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This post-natal development period is notably compressed relative to the extended incubation, a classic pattern among altricial birds where rapid nestling growth is prioritized to minimize vulnerability in the nest. Following fledging, a period of substantial somatic growth and behavioral maturation ensues. The time since birth at puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal recrudescence and full reproductive capacity, occurs at 78 days [tp = 78 days] at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. The relatively short interval between fledging and the attainment of sexual maturity suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes early entry into the breeding population, a trait commonly observed in small-bodied birds with high adult mortality.

Reproductive output in Sternoclyta cyanopectus has been characterized through detailed field observations of nesting activity. At a typical active body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], females are capable of producing two broods annually [F_R_i = two broods annually], each consisting of two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch]. This yields a maximum reproduction rate of approximately 2 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 2 offspring per year]. The two eggs per clutch represent a substantial energetic investment, each egg comprising a significant fraction of the female's own body mass. The two broods annually are typically spaced to coincide with peaks in nectar availability, ensuring adequate provisioning for the developing nestlings. This breeding schedule is typical of many Neotropical hummingbirds that exploit seasonally predictable floral resources in montane environments.

The timing of first reproduction is a pivotal component of the species' demography. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of active metabolism, with a core body temperature maintained at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the time since birth at first brood has been estimated at approximately 365 days [tR = approximately 365 days]. This indicates that most individuals defer their first breeding attempt until their second calendar year of life, a delay that allows for the complete acquisition of foraging skills and the establishment of a suitable territory in the competitive hummingbird community. The prolonged subadult stage contrasts with the rapid attainment of puberty at 78 days [tp = 78 days], suggesting that physiological maturity substantially precedes the behavioral and ecological conditions necessary for successful nesting at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This pattern of delayed first reproduction, despite early gonadal maturation, is a common feature in birds where territory ownership or access to a high-quality home range is critical for reproductive success.

Comparative data on longevity for the Violet-chested hummingbird remain scarce, but insights can be drawn from related species with similar life-history strategies. Based on records for the black-chinned hummingbird (Archilochus alexandri), a well-studied species of comparable body size, the maximum lifespan under field conditions can reach ten years [am = ten years] at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This value, recorded for a species that experiences similar metabolic rates and predation pressures, provides a useful benchmark for Sternoclyta cyanopectus. The attainment of a lifespan of ten years [am = ten years] would represent a remarkable 140-fold extension beyond the time taken to reach fledging, highlighting the substantial investment in somatic maintenance and survival that characterizes even the smallest endotherms at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. The high daily field metabolic rates associated with hovering flight dictate that hummingbirds operate under extreme energetic constraints, yet the ten year [am = ten year] lifespan demonstrates that these constraints are not incompatible with extended survivorship at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. Future studies focusing on capture-mark-recapture efforts within the species' restricted range are needed to refine this estimate.
